title.en: Kagsagsuk: The Persecuted Orphan and the Amarok
title.zh: 卡格薩克舒克：受虐孤兒與狼靈

region.zh: 西格陵蘭（格陵蘭及拉布拉多流本）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; collated from nine copies (Greenland and Labrador), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 1 'Kagsagsuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Persecuted by the whole settlement — lifted by the nostrils, teeth pulled, rolled in snow — the orphan Kagsagsuk calls 'Lord of strength' between two mountains, and the amarok wolf-spirit shakes seal-bones out of his body five times until he cannot be thrown. Trained daily in secret, he carries a driftwood spar on his shoulders by night, then splits, swings, and hurls three bears in front of the crowd; the same people who mocked him offer boots and seats, and he crushes them one by one, sparing only the kind, and roams the coast leaving marks of his great deeds.
summary.zh: 孤兒卡格薩克舒克受全村凌虐——被提鼻懸舉、拔牙禁刀、雪中翻滾——他在兩山之間呼喚『力之主』，狼靈阿馬洛克五次摔他，震出體內海豹小骨，直至他再也摔不倒。他夜半肩扛浮木示力，冰上連破三熊——拋擲如玩具——昔日施虐者爭相奉衣讓座，他逐一捏碎，獨饒善者；沿海岸炫耀神力，遺蹟至今猶存。

sensitivity.note: Rink collates nine copies; same tale-type as Rasmussen's Kagssagssuk (cross-ref inuit-kagssagssuk-homeless-boy). Graphic vengeance recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: There was once a poor orphan boy who lived among uncharitable men; his name was Kagsagsuk, and his foster-mother a miserable old woman. Their wretched shed adjoined the house-passage, and they were not allowed into the main room; Kagsagsuk did not even venture into the shed, but lay in the passage warming himself among the dogs, crying 'Na-ah! Na-ah!' mocking himself in imitation of them. The men lifted him above the threshold only by putting their fingers into his nostrils — these accordingly enlarged, but otherwise he did not grow at all. They gave him frozen meat without a knife, saying his teeth might do instead, and sometimes pulled out a couple of teeth, complaining of his eating too much; the boys rolled him in the snow filling his clothes with it, and the girls covered him all over with filth. At length he ventured out among the mountains by himself, choosing solitary places and meditating how to get strength, as his foster-mother had taught him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 1 'Kagsagsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Standing between two high mountains, he called out: 'Lord of strength, come forth! Lord of strength, come to me!' A large animal appeared in the shape of an amarok (a fabulous animal, originally a wolf); terrified, Kagsagsuk tried to run, but the beast overtook him and, twisting its tail round his body, threw him down — and a rustling sound followed as small seal-bones, like toys, fell from his own body. 'It is because of these bones that thy growth has been stopped,' said the amarok, and repeated the process: again bones fell, fewer each time, until the fifth throw he did not fall at all but jumped along the ground. 'If it be thy wish to become strong and vigorous, thou mayst come every day to me,' said the beast, adding that human beings would not be able to conquer him any more, but he had better stick to his old habits; when winter came and the sea was frozen, three great bears would appear, and they should be killed by his hand. He met the amarok every day, feeling stronger each time, kicking the very rocks on his way home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 1 'Kagsagsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At nightfall he asked for his mother's boots, slipped out, loosened the moorings of a great piece of driftwood the kayakers had been unable to carry up, flung the spar on his shoulders, and buried it behind the house; in the morning the whole settlement cried that there must be a man of extraordinary strength among them, the young men each giving themselves great airs — the impostors. Kagsagsuk stuck to his old habits until the sea froze. Then the men came running in to report three bears climbing an iceberg, and nobody dared attack them: now was his time. With his foster-mother's boots he ran through the crowd as if they had been a shoal of small fish, heels almost touching his neck, the snow sparkling in rainbow colours about him. Ascending the iceberg, he made himself hard — invulnerable by charm — and seizing the largest bear by the fore-paws flung it against the iceberg, the haunches severed from the body: 'This was my first catch; now, flense away and divide!' The second he threw down the same way; the third he swung above his head and hurled at the bystanders — 'This fellow behaved shamefully towards me!' — until they all fled before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 1 'Kagsagsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He brought the two bear-skins to his foster-mother — 'There is one for thy couch, and another for thy coverlet!' — ordered the flesh cooked, and was requested to enter the main room; peeping above the threshold as was his wont, 'I really can't get across, unless some one will lift me up by the nostrils' — and nobody else venturing, his old foster-mother came and lifted him as he desired. All the men now became very civil: 'Step forward,' 'Come and sit down, friend,' 'Here is a nice seat for Kagsagsuk,' and the girls rivalled each other in offering to make clothes for him. But at supper he squeezed the girl who fetched his water so hard the blood rushed from her mouth — 'Why, I think she is burst!' — while the parents meekly rejoined she was good for nothing but fetching water. The boys he called great future seal-hunters and crushed to death; others he killed by tearing their limbs asunder, and the parents only said, 'It does not signify — he was a good-for-nothing.' Thus he went on until the whole household had perished by his hand, sparing only the poor people who had been kind to him; taking the best kayak left, he roamed all over the country in the pride of his heart, and even nowadays marks of his great deeds are shown along the coast — which is why the history of Kagsagsuk is supposed to be true.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 1 'Kagsagsuk'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Blind Man Who Used His Mother for a Hunting-Bladder

region.zh: 西格陵蘭（格陵蘭及拉布拉多流本）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; collated from eight copies (Greenland and Labrador), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 2 'The Blind Man who recovered his Sight', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Witchcraft on a thong-seal skin blinds a son who wants it for hunting-lines; starved and cheated of his own bear-meat by his mother, he is cured by wild-geese droppings on his eyes at the lake. Feigning blindness, he tests her with three dreams, then makes her serve as his hunting-bladder at the white-whale hunt and pushes her into the sea — 'My ullo! It was I who nursed thee!' Her spreading hair turns to the narwhal's long teeth; brother and sister flee the deed into the interior, grow immensely old, and the man returns once to denounce himself in the moonlight before vanishing forever.
summary.zh: 母親在長鬚海豹皮上施咒，令取皮製獵繩的兒子雙目失明；她又私藏熊肉、以貝類餓他。湖畔雁糞落眼復明。他佯盲三次試母，繼而在白鯨獵中令母親充當浮囊，把她推入海中——『我的烏羅刀！是我養大你的！』其散髮化為一角鯨長牙。兄妹懼罪遁入內陸，壽至極高；男子最後一次現身月光下自陳其罪，從此絕跡。

sensitivity.note: Rink collates eight copies (two Labrador). Matricide and narwhal etiology recorded as told in the 1875 source; the angakok denunciation scene is a documented Greenlandic confession custom.

passages.text: A widow had a son and a daughter; the son grew up useful in different ways and commenced seal-hunting, and one day in early winter caught a thong-seal. His mother wanted the skin for a ledge-cover, but he insisted on having it for hunting-lines; angry, she prepared the skin, removing the hairs with witchcraft, saying: 'When he cuts thee into thongs, when he cuts thee asunder, then thou shalt snap and smite his face' — and rejoiced in the thought that it would hit him. When he cut out the first thong and scraped it with a shell, a small blister burst, hitting both his eyes and blinding him. The winter coming on destitute, they lived entirely on mussels, and the blind boy took his place on the ledge, unable to hunt. A great bear appeared eating away their window-pane and thrust its head into the room; the mother and sister fled in terror, but the blind man asked his sister for his bow and her right aim for him, shot, and the bear fell. The mother said, 'Thou hitst the window instead of the beast'; his sister whispered, 'Thou hast killed a bear.' Yet the mother never gave him any of the boiled bear-flesh, only shell-fish, concealing her having any flesh, to starve him; his sister gave him his portion in her absence, which he swallowed in haste.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 2 'The Blind Man who recovered his Sight'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In spring the sister reminded him how delightful it was when he could see and go hunting, and at daybreak they went out together, he holding her garments. At a large plain beside a lake he lay down while she went for fuel; wild geese flew overhead and one cried, 'Look at the poor young man down there; he is blind: would we could make him see.' Something warm fell on his eyes — the goose's excrement — and a voice said: 'Keep thy eyes shut till the sound of our wings has altogether passed away, then thou mayst try to open them.' The goose swept its wings across his face repeating 'Mind thou dost not open thy eyes.' When the noise had passed he opened his eyes wide and had his sight restored. His sister would not believe until she looked into his reopened eyes; they agreed not to let their mother know.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 2 'The Blind Man who recovered his Sight'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Approaching the house he caught sight of his bear-skin drying and its bones and paws; shutting his eyes, he took his place on the ledge, feigned sleep, and 'dreamed' three times — of the skin behind the house, the bones at the entrance, and two bear's paws under the couch — the mother repeating 'Thou must surely have been thinking about somebody who happened to hurt thee some time ago.' At the third dream, suddenly opening his eyes: 'Mother, I mean these' — and she knew he had regained his sight, exclaiming 'Eat them, just eat them!' He resumed seal-hunting, but the idea of revenge grew on him. At the white-whale season he hunted with his sister fastened as his hunting-bladder; and one day asked her if she liked their old mother — 'I am more fond of thee than of her; thou art the only one I do love.' 'Well, then, to-morrow she shall serve us for a bladder. I'll pay her off for having made me blind.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 2 'The Blind Man who recovered his Sight'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother declared herself willing and went down to the open sea with them next morning. When the white whales appeared she said, 'Take one of the smallest, and not the large ones,' crying out at the very little fish, 'Look out and try for one of these' — 'They are still too big,' he answered, and harpooned one of the very largest, letting go his hold of the line. When the animal had drawn his mother close to the water he cried, 'Dost thou remember the time thou madest me blind?' and pushed her on: 'That fellow will give me my revenge.' Close to the edge of the water she cried, 'My ullo! It was I who nursed thee' — and was plunged into the sea; still she reappeared crying 'My ullo, my ullo; I nursed thee!' then disappeared forever. It is said she was afterwards transformed into a fish, her spreading hair turning into long horny teeth, from which the narwhals are said to have their origin. Brother and sister, terrified at their deed, fled eastward to the large continent, he refusing at first to kill a bird for pity at their gift of sight, until he killed one swan for his sister — the only bird he caught for the rest of his life. They grew immensely old without friends; at last he went to an angakok's spirit-calling and denounced himself — 'I am that very man... do come out and see what I am like' — standing in the bright moonlight with hair snowy white as a hood of white hare-skins, face black, clothes of reindeer-skins. His sister could no longer move from old age; their house-fellows were terrible beings with heads like seals. 'After this, I will not show myself any more to human creatures; those to whom I wanted to denounce myself I have done it to.' He turned away and has never been seen afterwards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 2 'The Blind Man who recovered his Sight'; not verbatim.

title.en: Igimarasugsuk, the Wife-Eater, and the Magic Driftwood
title.zh: 食妻者伊基馬拉舒克與魔木

region.zh: 西格陵蘭（格陵蘭及拉布拉多流本）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; well known to every child in Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 3 'Igimarasugsuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Secretly killing and eating his wives and children, Igimarasugsuk murders his wife's little brother and forces her to share the meal. Fattened on reindeer-tallow till she cannot move, she rolls to a muddy pool, drinks herself lighter, stuffs her jacket as a decoy for his lance, and sings herself inside a great driftwood log that opens at her spell. Traced to the log, the fox-hole, and the bushes, he laments at every dead end — 'Oh what a pity I put off eating her so long!' — until she reaches berry-gatherers and safety.
summary.zh: 伊基馬拉舒克暗殺並吞食歷任妻子與子女；他殺害妻弟逼妻子同食。他以馴鹿脂油將妻子餵至不能動彈；她滾至泥塘飲水瘦身，以絮衣假人誘其長矛，再唱咒使巨木開合藏身。蹤跡屢斷於巨木、狐穴、灌木叢——他每到一處便哀嘆『可惜當初不早些吃掉她！』——直至她抵達採莓人群而脫身。

sensitivity.note: Rink notes this tale is known to every child in Greenland. Same tale-type as Rasmussen's Imarasugssuaq (cross-ref inuit-imarasugssuaq-wife-eater). Cannibalism recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: It was said of Igimarasugsuk that he always lost his wives in a very short time, and always as quickly married again; but nobody knew that he always killed and ate his wives, as well as his little children. At last he married a girl who had a younger brother and many relatives besides. Returning from a reindeer-hunt, he one day sent his brother-in-law to fetch his axe from underneath the boat-pillars — and followed him; on hearing her brother's shrieks, the wife peeped out and beheld him pursuing the boy, striking him on the head so that he fell dead on the spot. He then ordered his wife to dress and boil parts of her brother's body, and commenced eating, offering her a piece of an arm and insisting she eat with him; she only feigned to do so, concealing her portion under the ashes of the fire. 'I actually think thou art crying!' exclaimed the husband. 'No,' she said, 'I am only a little shy.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 3 'Igimarasugsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After devouring his brother-in-law he began to fatten his wife, ordering her to eat nothing but reindeer-tallow and drink only what a small shell would hold, until she grew so fat she could not move about at all. One day he went away, having securely shut the entrance to the summer-tent and fastened it with strong cords. When he had been gone a considerable time she took her knife, let herself fall from the bench, and rolled herself as far as the entry; by great efforts she crossed the threshold, cut the strings fastening the outer curtain, rolled down to a muddy pool and drank a great deal of water, after which she felt less heavy and was able to get up and walk back. She re-entered the tent, stuffed out her jacket, put it on the bench with its back turned outward, fastened the entrance well, and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 3 'Igimarasugsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Convinced her husband would pursue her, she went down to a very large piece of drift-wood hauled ashore and worked a spell upon it, singing: 'KissugssuaK pingerssuaK, ia-ha-ha, arape, Kupe, sipe, sipe sisaria' — and forthwith the timber opened midways and she entered it, again singing, and it closed around her in darkness. She heard her husband coming: he had entered the tent and thrust his lance into the stuffed jacket, and discovering what it really was, ran out, following her footprints all the way to the timber, where she plainly heard him say: 'Oh what a pity I waited so long in killing her! oh poor miserable me!' Every trace ending at the timber, he went away; she sang the timber open, crept out, and ran on, hiding herself in a fox-hole — where every trace again ended, and she heard him digging the very earth with his hands before tiring and going away, returning and bemoaning himself in the same manner.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 3 'Igimarasugsuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Taking refuge behind some bushes, she again heard the old lament — 'What a pity I put off eating her so long!' — 'Here every trace of her ends.' At length she caught sight of people gathering berries; on perceiving her they were about to take fright, when she cried out, 'I am the wife of Igimarasugsuk,' and they approached her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 3 'Igimarasugsuk'; not verbatim.
